analysis.one_liner: Creates a national paid family and medical leave insurance program funded by a small payroll tax.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 36 senators including the majority leader, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in May 2023 and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The FAMILY Act would create a federal paid family and medical leave program run by the Social Security Administration. Workers who need time off to care for a new child, a seriously ill family member, their own serious health condition, or to deal with domestic violence or stalking could receive a monthly benefit — up to $4,000 a month at the top, $580 at the bottom, prorated for days of caregiving. It would be funded at first by an appropriation from the Treasury, then permanently by a new payroll tax of 0.2% on employees and 0.2% on employers (0.4% total on self-employment income). States that already run their own paid leave programs would get federal grants to keep them going.
analysis.who_benefits: Working people and their families: nearly any worker or self-employed person who needs paid time to care for a newborn, a seriously ill relative, or their own serious illness, or to escape domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking. Benefits replace a large share of wages — 85% of earnings up to about $1,257 a month, then lower percentages — with a minimum of $580 a month, adjusted upward over time. Employers must restore the worker to their job (or an equivalent one) and keep their health coverage during leave, and retaliation against someone who takes leave is unlawful. States with existing paid leave programs would receive federal grants covering their costs, and employers who provide the benefit under those state laws could share in the grant.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers needing paid family or medical leave

how_it_helps.text: Creates a federal paid leave insurance benefit of at least $580 and up to $4,000 per month, prorated by days of caregiving, for workers caring for a new child, a seriously ill family member, their own serious health condition, or dealing with domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking [S2].

Covers a broad circle of family members, including domestic partners, siblings, grandparents, and grandchildren, and includes self-employed workers, who pay a 0.4% self-employment tax to participate [S2].

Requires employers to restore a worker to their position (or an equivalent one) after leave, keep health coverage in place during leave, and makes retaliation within 12 months of taking leave a rebuttable presumption of unlawful retaliation, enforceable in court with damages and attorney's fees [S2].

Gives states that already run comprehensive paid leave programs ('legacy states') federal grants equal to their benefit and administration costs, so they keep their programs without losing federal funding [S2].

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, employers would pay a new 0.2% excise tax on wages, and employees would pay 0.2% of wages; self-employed people would pay 0.4% of self-employment income. The first three years of benefits and administration would be paid by a Treasury appropriation that must be repaid within 10 years. Employers would also bear the cost of holding jobs open and maintaining health coverage during leave. Workers who take leave would see their benefit reduced by any workers' compensation or unemployment benefits they receive, and by state paid-leave benefits under coordination rules.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers and workers via payroll tax

drawbacks.text: The funding is a new permanent payroll tax: 0.2% on employers and 0.2% on employees (0.4% on self-employment income), a recurring cost on every covered wage that falls on businesses and reduces workers' take-home pay [S2].

Benefits are capped at 20 caregiving days per month and 60 days per 12-month benefit period, so a worker needing a full year of care (such as a long recovery or extended newborn care) would exhaust the benefit before the year ends [S2].

Employers must keep the job open and maintain group health coverage for the worker during leave, a real cost for small employers with limited staffing, and the anti-retaliation presumption makes any adverse action within 12 months of leave presumptively unlawful, which employers' groups would argue invites litigation [S2].

Because the first three years are funded by a Treasury appropriation that must be repaid within 10 years, the program starts on borrowed money and its long-term cost falls entirely on the new payroll tax [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers without any paid leave — the majority of the U.S. workforce at the time — the benefit is substantial: up to roughly a year's worth of partial wage replacement (capped at 60 days) with job protection, for a tax that totals 0.4% of wages split between worker and employer, comparable to state programs already operating in several states. The main honest objection is the new permanent payroll tax and the compliance burden on employers, especially small businesses, plus the 60-day cap that limits the benefit for long recoveries. The design closely mirrors state programs that have functioned for years, which supports the case that it is workable, though the federal scale and start-up financing carry added risk.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the same day, May 18, 2023; the committee never took it up, and it died there when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Gillibrand introduced the FAMILY Act on May 18, 2023, with 31 other Democratic senators joining as original cosponsors [S2].
The same day it was introduced, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance — the last action ever taken on the bill [S4].
A total of 36 senators cosponsored the bill: 35 of the 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of the 4 independents. No Republican signed on [S3].
The Finance Committee held no hearing, markup, or vote on the bill through the end of the 118th Congress [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have paid the 0.2% payroll tax and held jobs and health coverage open during leave are better off; workers needing paid leave are no better off than before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who avoided the payroll tax

for.name: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 35 cosponsors; led its only push for consideration.

for.name: Sen. Chuck Schumer
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as one of its 31 original cosponsors.

for.name: 35 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it the support of roughly three-quarters of the Senate Democratic caucus.

against.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill on the day of introduction and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 36 cosponsors were Democrats or independents; no Republican signed on, and the bill never advanced past committee referral.

industries.note: Employers would pay a new 0.2% payroll tax on wages and must hold jobs open and maintain health coverage during a worker's leave, with a court-enforceable anti-retaliation presumption. Because the benefit replaces wages workers would otherwise forgo, workers and employers both gain leave coverage but both share the tax cost.

industries.industry: States with existing paid leave programs ('legacy states')
industries.note: States like California, New York, and New Jersey that already run comprehensive paid leave programs would receive federal grants equal to their benefit and administration costs, effectively federalizing their funding. Workers in those states keep their existing benefits at no added federal cost to the state.

industries.industry: Employers and insurers administering benefits in legacy states
industries.note: In states that let employers provide paid leave benefits directly or through insurers and multiemployer plans, the bill counts those benefits as the state program and allows states to share the federal grant with them, locking in that role.
